before.title: 5-Speed Automatic Torque Converter Lockup Shudder
before.description: Second-generation Pilots with the 5-speed automatic develop a torque-converter lockup-clutch shudder felt as a brief vibration or 'rumble-strip' shake, typically during light acceleration around 25 mph or while cruising at 55-65 mph when the converter clutch partially engages/slips. The cause is the lockup clutch failing to apply smoothly, aggravated by aged or degraded ATF. Left unaddressed it accelerates converter and clutch wear.
before.solution: Perform a Honda DW-1 ATF drain-and-fill (often two or three cycles) to restore fluid condition; many owners report the shudder clears with fresh fluid. Persistent cases require torque-converter replacement (updated/revised converters address the early defect). Use only Honda DW-1 ATF — non-spec fluid worsens the shudder.
symptoms: Vibration/shudder under light acceleration around 25 mph
Rumble or shake while cruising 55-65 mph
Feels like driving over rumble strips
Symptom comes and goes with throttle and converter lockup

before.title: AC Clutch Relay Failure Causing No Cold Air or Battery Drain
before.description: The Omron A/C clutch relay (Honda part 39794-SDA-A03) is defective and gets hot, causing failure. Honda-specific part with reduced coil current known to be problematic. When relay fails, either battery dies overnight (relay stuck closed) or AC stops working (relay stuck open). Low refrigerant from pressure relief valve venting can lead to failed AC compressor.
before.solution: Replace defective Omron relay (39794-SDA-A03) with updated Mitsuba relay (39794-SDA-A05) at dealer ($20-$40 part + $50-$100 labor) or DIY (relay in engine bay fuse box). If AC still not working, check refrigerant level and recharge ($150-$200). If clutch physically failed, full compressor replacement required ($1,200-$1,900).
symptoms: AC compressor not engaging (no click when AC turned on)

before.title: Auto Idle Stop Engine Fails to Auto-Restart (No-Restart / Stall at Stop)
before.description: On third-gen Pilots with the J35Y6 V6 and ZF 9-speed automatic, the Auto Idle Stop (engine stop-start) system shuts the engine off at a stop but the engine then fails to automatically restart when the driver releases the brake, leaving the vehicle dead in traffic and sometimes requiring a jump start. NHTSA opened Preliminary Evaluation PE22-005 in June 2022 (221 complaints, ~194,000 vehicles) and in March 2025 upgraded it to Engineering Analysis EA25-004 covering roughly 2.2 million Honda/Acura vehicles. Honda traces it to weak 12V battery charge state, the battery current/IBS sensor, and brake-booster vacuum/PGM-FI logic that prevents a clean restart.
before.solution: Honda issued TSBs 23-008 and 23-009 (and warranty extension 23-009) providing a two-stage remedy: a PGM-FI/idle-stop control software update, and if the no-restart persists, battery and 12V battery sensor inspection/replacement. Many owners disable Auto Idle Stop each drive as a workaround. Replace a weak OEM battery proactively; have the software update applied and confirm the battery sensor is calibrated.
symptoms: Engine shuts off at stop and does not auto-restart
Have to shift to Park and restart manually or jump start
Dashboard warning lights/flicker during failed restart
Hesitation or stall when pulling away from a light

before.title: Automatic Transmission 2nd-Gear Overheating and Torque Converter Failure
before.description: Early first-generation Pilot models share a well-documented 5-speed automatic transmission weakness with other Honda/Acura trucks of the era. Honda issued a safety recall to install an oil jet intended to improve lubrication/cooling of second gear because inadequate lubrication could lead to gear overheating, discoloration, breakage, and eventual transmission failure or lockup. Owners commonly report slipping, harsh shifting, flashing D4, burnt fluid, and complete loss of drive, sometimes even after the recall if damage had already begun.
before.solution: Verify whether the recall was completed and inspect for signs of overheated or contaminated ATF, delayed engagement, and shift flare. Scan the transmission control system for ratio and pressure-related codes, road test for slipping or flare on the 1-2 and 2-3 shifts, and inspect line pressure if needed. Mild cases may improve temporarily with repeated drain-and-fill using the correct Honda ATF, but many units ultimately require rebuild or replacement if second gear or the torque converter is damaged.

before.title: Parasitic Battery Drain Causing Dead Battery
before.description: Honda Pilots experience excessive parasitic battery drain (over 80mA) causing dead batteries after 24-48 hours. Common causes include radio/audio staying active when off, Bluetooth module constantly searching, and AC compressor clutch relay sticking on. Normal draw should be 12-30mA. Vehicle requires 30+ minutes to fully "fall asleep" with hood, doors, and trunk closed.

Disconnect or replace Bluetooth/hands-free module if causing drain. Test parasitic draw with multimeter after 30+ minutes. Replace weak battery. Check three main ground connections for oxidation/corrosion.

Clicking sound when trying to start

before.title: A/C Condenser Leak at Receiver/Dryer Cap — No Cold Air
before.description: Third-gen Pilots lose A/C cooling because the parallel-flow condenser leaks refrigerant (R-1234yf) at the lower corner around the receiver/dryer cap, due to poor O-ring compression against the receiver/dryer barrel wall. Honda documents this in Service Bulletin 18-080. Owners report the system blows warm within a season or two and the low side pumps down empty quickly; the corner near the dryer cap is often stained with oily refrigerant dye. (A leaking A/C compressor shaft seal can mimic the same no-cold-air symptom.)
before.solution: Per TSB 18-080, replace the receiver/dryer cap O-ring (or the condenser/receiver-dryer assembly if damaged), evacuate and recharge the system with R-1234yf. Note these 2016-2018 Pilots are NOT covered by Honda's 10-year condenser warranty extension applied to some other models, so repairs are typically out of pocket.
symptoms: A/C blows warm or only cools intermittently
Refrigerant leaks down within months of a recharge
Oily/dye stain at the lower condenser corner near the receiver/dryer cap

before.title: Catalytic Converter Efficiency Failure Triggering P0420 / P0430
before.description: The Pilot's three-way catalytic converters lose conversion efficiency with age and contamination, setting P0420 (Bank 1) and/or P0430 (Bank 2) and illuminating the check engine light. Symptoms include reduced power/fuel economy, a rotten-egg (sulfur) smell, and a rattle from a broken internal substrate. Note: on 2016-2018 Pilots these catalyst codes are very often caused upstream by failing fuel injectors (covered by Honda TSB 20-100 and a 10yr/150k warranty extension), so a full diagnosis is essential before condemning the converter.
before.solution: Diagnose before replacing: verify upstream/downstream O2 sensor behavior and rule out injectors (especially 2016-2018) and exhaust leaks. If the converter is genuinely failed, replace with an OEM or CARB-compliant unit for the affected bank. Address any root cause (oil consumption/VCM, misfires, rich condition) so the new converter is not damaged.
symptoms: Check engine light with P0420 or P0430

before.title: Door Lock Actuator Failure — Doors Won't Lock/Unlock or Cycle Randomly
before.description: Individual door lock actuators fail so a door stops responding to the key fob or lock switch, sometimes working in only one direction (locks but won't unlock, or vice versa), and can produce repeated clicking or random lock/unlock cycling. before.title: Front Brake Rotor Warping and Brake Judder Under Moderate Braking
before.description: Brake pulsation from front rotor thickness variation is one of the most commonly reported Pilot complaints across both generations. Owners describe steering wheel shake and pedal pulsation during highway-speed braking, often recurring after inexpensive pad-and-rotor jobs if hub runout, caliper slide condition, or lug torque is ignored. The Pilot's weight and heat load can make low-quality rotors especially prone to repeat judder.
before.solution: Confirm the vibration occurs only during braking, then measure rotor thickness variation and check hub runout, caliper slide pins, and pad wear pattern. Replace rotors and pads with quality parts, clean rust from the hub face, lubricate slide pins, torque wheels evenly by hand to spec, and flush old brake fluid if caliper drag is suspected. If pulsation returns quickly, inspect for sticking calipers or rear brake imbalance contributing to front overheating.
symptoms: vibration at highway speeds only during braking

communityRecommendations.content: Ask the shop to measure hub runout and clean the hub face before installing new rotors; many repeat failures are caused by mounting surfaces, not just rotor quality.

Owners often report better durability from coated premium rotors than bargain economy rotors.
Ceramic pads are commonly paired with premium rotors to reduce noise and provide stable braking feel.

before.title: Front Suspension Compliance Bushing and Lower Control Arm Wear Causing Clunks and Tire Wear
before.description: First-generation Pilots commonly develop worn front compliance bushings and lower control arm bushings, leading to clunking over bumps, vague steering feel, braking instability, and uneven front tire wear. before.title: Power Liftgate Strut and Motor Failure — Tailgate Won't Stay Open or Cycles Closed
before.description: On power-liftgate Pilots the gas-charged support struts weaken and lose nitrogen pressure prematurely, so they no longer help lift or hold the heavy tailgate. This forces the power motor to carry the full load, which leads to the liftgate opening then immediately closing, grinding/beeping, stopping partway, or refusing to open or close. A very common misdiagnosis is replacing the motor when weak struts are the real cause.
before.solution: First try the reset procedure (Park, hold the dash tailgate button until it starts opening, press to stop, then close from the liftgate button). Replace the gas support struts as a pair first (inexpensive, often the true fix); if the gate still binds or the motor grinds, replace the power liftgate motor/actuator assembly. Verify strut pressure before ordering a motor.

before.title: Rear A/C Blows Warm — Clogged Rear Expansion Valve / Evaporator or Stuck Rear Blend Door
before.description: On the Pilot's dual-zone rear A/C system, the front vents blow cold but the rear vents blow warm. Common causes are a clogged or stuck-closed rear expansion valve (starving the rear evaporator of refrigerant), a plugged rear evaporator, or a stuck rear blend-door actuator holding the rear in the heat position. A dirty screen on the rear blower can also reduce cooling. It is a widely reported complaint on family-hauler Pilots.
before.solution: Diagnose the rear circuit separately from the front: verify refrigerant reaches the rear evaporator (check the rear expansion valve for clog/stick), inspect the rear blend-door actuator movement, and clean the rear blower intake screen. Replace the expansion valve, rear actuator, or (worst case) the rear evaporator as indicated, then evacuate and recharge.
symptoms: Front A/C cold but rear vents blow warm
Weak or no cooling from rear vents
Rear blows hot even with rear A/C on
Uneven cabin temperature front to rear

before.description: Second-gen Pilots are prone to starter-motor and starter-cable degradation: owners report a single click or slow/no crank, often with a corroded or burnt main copper starter cable terminal as the failure point. before.title: Tailgate/Rear Hatch Wiring Harness Breaks Causing Inoperative Rear Lights, Lock, or Glass Release
before.description: On first-generation Pilots, repeated opening and closing of the rear hatch can fatigue and break wires inside the hatch harness near the hinge or rubber boot. Owners report intermittent or failed rear license plate lights, rear wiper, rear glass release, power lock, or tailgate-related electrical functions. The issue is typically caused by copper conductors fracturing inside intact-looking insulation.
before.solution: Inspect the hatch harness where it flexes at the top of the liftgate, peeling back the rubber boot and tug-testing each wire. Repair involves soldering in new wire sections or replacing the damaged harness, then sealing the repair to prevent moisture intrusion. Because multiple circuits can fail at once, continuity testing each affected wire is usually faster than replacing individual components.

before.title: Valve Cover Gasket and Spark Plug Tube Seal Oil Leak Causing Misfires
before.description: On the J35 V6, the rubber valve cover gaskets and the integrated spark plug tube seals harden and shrink with age and heat, allowing oil to weep onto the hot exhaust manifolds (burning-oil smell) and, more seriously, to pool down inside the spark plug wells. Oil saturates the ignition coil boots and shorts the spark, producing misfires and a Check Engine Light. The rear (firewall-side) bank is hardest to access, so the leak is often neglected until misfires appear.
before.solution: Replace both valve cover gaskets and the spark plug tube seals (gasket sets include the tube seals); clean oil from the spark plug wells and inspect/replace any oil-soaked ignition coil boots and fouled spark plugs. Parts are inexpensive ($40-$80 per set) but labor is significant on the rear bank.
symptoms: Burning oil smell from the engine bay
Oily residue/grime on top of the valve covers
Oil pooled in the spark plug wells
Rough idle, misfire, and Check Engine Light
Occasional blue smoke / slightly higher oil consumption

before.title: VTM-4 Rear Differential Clutch Judder and Noise When Turning
before.description: AWD Pilots use Honda's VTM-4 rear differential, whose internal hydraulic clutch packs make a shudder/judder and noise during low-speed tight turns (e.g., parking lots, U-turns) when the VTM-4 differential fluid degrades or becomes contaminated by clutch-friction particles and/or condensation. Honda documents the condition in a service bulletin and a figure-eight diagnostic test. Water can also enter through the rear-subframe vent-tube breather after wading or boat launching, turning the fluid pink — in which case a flush may not fully cure the judder.
before.solution: Drain and refill with genuine Honda VTM-4 differential fluid (~5.6 qt for AWD); never substitute generic gear oil. Honda's flat-rate diagnosis uses ten figure-eight turns at full lock to confirm engagement/disengagement. Service the VTM-4 fluid every ~30,000 miles. If fluid is pink (water intrusion) or judder persists after fresh fluid, the clutch packs/differential may need replacement.
symptoms: Shudder/judder felt through the floor during tight low-speed turns
Groaning or binding noise in parking-lot maneuvers
Worse when fully warmed or on dry pavement

before.title: Water Intrusion Through Roof Seams or Sunroof Drains Causing Wet Headliner and Electrical Problems
before.description: Owners across both generations report water leaks into the cabin, commonly from clogged sunroof drains, deteriorated roof seam sealer, windshield perimeter leaks, or rear body seam leaks. Symptoms include wet headliners, damp carpets, musty odor, water in the overhead console area, and occasional electrical issues when moisture reaches connectors or modules. On older first-generation trucks, seam sealer shrinkage and body aging are frequent contributors.
before.solution: Perform a controlled water test beginning at the roof, windshield, and sunroof cassette drains, then inspect headliner and pillar trim for water tracks. Clear sunroof drains with low-pressure air or flexible line, reseal failed roof/body seams with automotive seam sealer, and repair windshield or hatch-area leaks as needed. Dry the carpet and inspect under-seat and pillar connectors to prevent corrosion-related electrical faults.

communityRecommendations.content: Do not use high-pressure compressed air on sunroof drains; it can disconnect the drain tube inside the pillar and make the leak worse.
After fixing the leak source, pull up the carpet padding and dry it fully because trapped moisture can linger for weeks and corrode connectors.
Flexible drain-cleaning line is commonly used to clear sunroof drains without damaging the tubes.
Automotive seam sealer is often used when roof or body seams are identified as the leak path.
